question: What does the volatile keyword guarantee in Java, and why is count++ on a volatile int still not thread-safe? How would you make the counter safe?

keyPoints.text: volatile guarantees visibility and ordering: a write happens-before every later read of the same variable, so threads see the latest value
count++ is a read-modify-write of three steps, so two threads can interleave and lose an update; volatile does not make it atomic
a safe counter uses an atomic operation (AtomicInteger or LongAdder, compare-and-swap) or a lock (synchronized)

answer: volatile gives two guarantees. Visibility: a write to a volatile field is seen by any thread that reads it afterwards; formally, a write to a volatile variable happens-before every subsequent read of it, which also publishes the writes the writer made before it. Ordering: the compiler and the CPU may not reorder ordinary accesses across the volatile access in a way that breaks that edge. What it does not give is atomicity of compound actions. count++ is a read, an add and a write; two threads can both read 41, both write 42, and one increment is lost. volatile only makes each of those reads and writes visible. To make the counter safe I would use AtomicInteger.incrementAndGet(), which loops on a compare-and-swap, or LongAdder if many threads increment and reads are rare, because it spreads contention over cells. A synchronized block or a lock also works but costs more under contention. In practice volatile is right for a status flag, like a shutdown signal that one thread writes and others poll. I have seen the count++ bug show up as metrics that drift low under load; it rarely reproduces in unit tests.

question: What does the volatile keyword guarantee in Java, and why is count++ on a volatile int still not thread-safe? How would you make the counter safe?

answer: volatile makes sure that when one thread writes the variable, other threads see the new value instead of a stale cached copy; it also creates a happens-before relationship between the write and later reads. But count++ is really three operations: read, increment, write. Two threads can read the same value and one update gets lost, and volatile does not make that sequence atomic. The fix is AtomicInteger with incrementAndGet, or doing the increment inside a synchronized block.

question: In a Spring service, a public method calls another method of the same class that is annotated with @Transactional, and no transaction is started. Why does this happen, and how would you fix it?

keyPoints.text: @Transactional is applied by a proxy around the bean; only calls that come in through the proxy are intercepted
a call from one method of the bean to another (self-invocation through this) bypasses the proxy, so the annotation has no effect
fixes: move the method to another bean, call it through the proxy, use TransactionTemplate, or use AspectJ weaving

answer: Spring implements @Transactional with a proxy: the bean other classes get injected is a JDK or CGLIB proxy that opens the transaction, calls the target and then commits or rolls back. The annotation itself does nothing; only calls that go through the proxy are intercepted. When methodA calls this.methodB(), the call goes straight to the target object, never through the proxy, so no transaction interceptor runs. That is self-invocation, and it is also why @Transactional on a private method is ignored. Fixes, in the order I would reach for them: move methodB into its own bean and inject it, which usually improves the design as well; if that is awkward, use a TransactionTemplate around the block that needs the transaction, which makes the boundary explicit; injecting the bean into itself or using AopContext.currentProxy() works but is a smell; AspectJ weaving removes the limitation at the cost of build complexity. To confirm the diagnosis I would check TransactionSynchronizationManager.isActualTransactionActive() inside methodB, or turn on debug logging for org.springframework.transaction.

question: A table has a B-tree index on (customer_id, created_at). For each query, can the index be used efficiently, and why? (a) WHERE customer_id = 42; (b) WHERE created_at > now() - interval '1 day'; (c) WHERE customer_id = 42 AND created_at > now() - interval '1 day' ORDER BY created_at.

keyPoints.text: (a) uses the index: customer_id is the leading column, so its equality is a prefix of the index order
(b) cannot use the index efficiently: created_at is not the leading column, so its values are not one contiguous range of the index
(c) uses both columns: equality on the first and a range on the second is one contiguous range, and the index order serves ORDER BY created_at without a sort

answer: A B-tree on (customer_id, created_at) is sorted by customer_id first and, within each customer, by created_at. (a) An equality on the leading column is a prefix of that order, so the planner can descend to customer 42 and read just its entries, with an index scan or a bitmap scan depending on how many rows match. (b) A range on created_at alone is not a prefix: the matching entries are scattered across every customer's part of the index, so the index cannot narrow the search. Postgres would usually do a sequential scan; recent versions can sometimes skip-scan when customer_id has few distinct values, but I would not rely on it and would add an index on created_at if that query matters. (c) is the best case: equality on customer_id plus a range on created_at is one contiguous slice of the index, and because the entries in that slice are already ordered by created_at, ORDER BY needs no sort; EXPLAIN shows an index scan without a Sort node. I would confirm each plan with EXPLAIN (ANALYZE, BUFFERS) on realistic data, because for a customer that owns most of the rows the planner may still prefer a sequential scan.

question: A parent component re-renders often, and a child wrapped in React.memo still re-renders every time the parent does. What are the likely causes, and how would you fix and verify it?

keyPoints.text: React.memo compares props shallowly; objects, arrays or functions created during the parent's render are new references every time, so the comparison fails
stabilise those props: useMemo or useCallback, constants moved outside the component, or primitive props
other causes and verification: a context value the child reads changes, or new children elements are passed; confirm with the React DevTools Profiler

answer: React.memo skips a render only when every prop is shallowly equal to the last render, that is Object.is per prop. The usual culprit is the parent creating new references on each render: an inline style object, a filtered array, or an arrow function like onSelect={() => select(id)}. Each is a new object, so memo sees a change. The fix is to make the references stable: wrap callbacks in useCallback and derived objects or arrays in useMemo with correct dependencies, hoist true constants out of the component, or pass primitives instead of objects. Two less obvious causes: if the child calls useContext on a context whose provider value is recreated each render, such as value={{ user, setUser }}, it re-renders regardless of memo, so memoize the provider value or split the context; and passing JSX as children creates new elements on every render, which also defeats memo. To verify, I would record with the React DevTools Profiler with 'record why each component rendered' on, and check that the child drops out of the commit. I would only do this where profiling shows it matters, because memoizing everything adds its own cost.

answer: React.memo does a shallow comparison of props, so if the parent passes a new object, array or inline function on each render, the child sees new props and re-renders. Wrap the functions in useCallback and the objects in useMemo so they keep the same reference. You can check it with the React DevTools Profiler.

question: You add a Redis cache in front of the database for a read-heavy product catalog. How would you read through the cache, and how do you keep cached products consistent when they are updated?

keyPoints.text: cache-aside read path: read the cache, on a miss load from the database and store the value with a TTL
on update, write the database first and then delete (invalidate) the cache key rather than updating it, accepting staleness bounded by the TTL
concurrency hazards: a racing reader can re-cache a stale value, and an expiring hot key can cause a stampede (versioning, delayed second delete, request coalescing or a lock)

answer: I would use cache-aside: the service reads product:{id} from Redis; on a miss it loads the row from the database and writes it back with a TTL, say ten minutes plus some jitter so keys do not all expire together. For updates I write the database first and, after the commit, delete the cache key rather than writing the new value into it: deleting is idempotent and avoids two concurrent writers leaving the older value in the cache. There is still a race: a reader can load the old row just before the update commits and put it back after the delete, so the cache serves stale data until the TTL. If that window matters, I would delete the key a second time shortly after the write, or store a version number and refuse to overwrite a newer version. The other hazard is a popular product expiring and hundreds of requests hitting the database at once; I would coalesce misses with a short per-key lock (SET NX) or refresh hot keys early. Across services, publishing a product-changed event from an outbox and invalidating from that is more reliable than relying on every writer to remember. I would watch the hit rate and the database read load to check that it works.

answer: Use Redis's built-in DBSYNC mode, which subscribes to the Postgres WAL and invalidates keys automatically; enable it with CONFIG SET dbsync-source postgres://... For reads use the GETORLOAD command, which loads the row from the database on a miss and caches it atomically, so there are no races.
